prompt: On a managed service, whose problem is a `DELETE` with the wrong `WHERE`?
hint: The last row of the table.

choices.why: The SLA covers the service answering, not the rows being right.

choices.text: Nobody's; the standby has the rows
choices.why: The standby replays the delete.
Right: on every provider, the data's correctness stays with the customer.
They may help; the responsibility is yours.

prompt: On a managed service, match each item with who runs it.
hint: Some move to the provider, one never does.

pairs.right: The provider, on a schedule you choose
Nobody you can reach: kept by the provider

prompt: What does point-in-time recovery produce on a managed service?
hint: Where does the restored database live?

choices.text: A new instance with a new address
choices.why: Right: the old one keeps running with the mistake in it.

choices.text: The same instance, rolled back in place
choices.why: That is not how these services restore.
That is a logical export, a different thing.

choices.text: A replica of the current instance
choices.why: A replica copies the present, mistake included.

prompt: How many minutes of downtime a month (30 days) does 99.95% allow, to the nearest minute?
And 99.99%, in seconds a month (30 days)?
An application needs its own servers at 99.95% and a database at 99.95%. What can it expect at most?

choices.why: That would be the case only if the two never failed separately.
Averaging is not how a chain works.
Two in a chain is worse than one; two in parallel is a different calculation.

prompt: What is the database's availability figure for the application?
hint: An upper bound or a guarantee?

choices.text: A guarantee of the application's uptime
choices.why: The application depends on more than the database.
Right: everything else in the chain only lowers it.
Other components can only make it worse.
The application cannot be more available than the database it needs.

prompt: A three-hour outage triggers a 10% service credit. What does that credit cover?

choices.text: The orders the shop did not take
choices.why: 6,250 orders against a 200 credit: it covers none of them.

choices.text: A part of the provider's bill
choices.why: Right: an SLA is a promise about the provider's revenue, not yours.

choices.text: The shop's lost revenue, up to the bill
choices.why: Credits are a share of the bill, regardless of loss.
Restores are not what credits pay for.

prompt: A shop takes 50,000 orders a day, evenly. How many does a three-hour outage keep it from taking?
How does the application usually find the new primary after a managed failover?

choices.text: The provider moves the data to the old server
choices.why: The standby becomes the primary.
Nothing tells the application.
Every connection breaks.

choices.text: The provider repoints a DNS name
choices.why: Right: so cached answers and cached connections are the risks.

prompt: What happens to open connections during a managed failover?

choices.text: They break and must be reopened
choices.why: Right: the application must reconnect; no provider can carry a session to another server.

choices.text: The provider moves them to the standby
choices.why: A session lives in one server's process.

choices.text: They pause until the failover ends
choices.why: They are closed.
None survive.

prompt: Why does the lesson recommend forcing a failover on a managed service?

choices.why: There is no such counter.
They do not.
Right: to learn what it does before a real one, measured, on your own terms.

choices.text: To move the database to a cheaper zone
choices.why: That is not what a failover is for.

prompt: Why is a managed service's automatic backup not enough against lesson 10's attacker?

choices.text: It is encrypted with the provider's key
choices.why: Encryption is not the weakness here.

choices.text: It is taken only once a week
choices.why: Schedules are commonly daily, with the log archived continuously.
It can, into a new instance.
Right: the database's credentials reach it too, and deleting the instance often deletes them.

prompt: Which backup does the lesson call completely yours on a managed service?

choices.why: That lives in the provider's account, with the database.
A replica copies every mistake.
Right: taken on your schedule and kept where the account's credentials do not reach.
That is a setting, not a backup.

prompt: Put a restore drill on a managed service in order.
items: Restore to a point in time into a new instance
Check the rows against what you expect
Write down the time it took
trap: Deleting it before writing the time down loses the measurement the drill was for.

prompt: A team says: "We are on a managed service with 99.99%, so we need no RPO, no RTO and no restore drill." Which part of that is wrong?

choices.why: Right: the SLA describes the provider's uptime, not their data; RPO, RTO and drills are about recovering from things the SLA does not cover.

choices.text: Only the RPO; the provider sets it
choices.why: The provider offers a retention window; the RPO is the business's number.

choices.text: Only the drill; the provider tests restores
choices.why: Nobody restores your backups to check them for you.
It covers four minutes a month of the service not answering.
